screens.title: Understanding Materials and Textures
screens.narratorSegment: In 3D rendering, the shape of a model is only half the story. The material is the surface definition that tells the renderer how that shape interacts with light. Textures are image maps that feed a material with color, bump, metalness and other surface detail. In this chapter you will learn how Unity’s Standard shader implements Physically Based Rendering, why separate maps like Albedo, Normal, Metallic and Smoothness matter, and how to avoid common mistakes like blurry or incorrectly imported textures. We will walk through creating a material, configuring texture import settings, and applying a PBR texture set to a model so you can see direct cause and effect. A practical focus will help you balance visual fidelity and performance when choosing texture resolution. By the end you’ll be able to create a PBR material, know what each map contributes, and fix frequent issues that make assets look wrong in a scene. Think of materials as the skin and textures as the decals that give that skin its specific, believable detail.

screens.title: Materials vs Textures
screens.narratorSegment: A material is the set of properties that define how a surface looks and how it interacts with light. Think of it as the object's skin: it holds color values, reflective behavior, transparency, and how rough or smooth the surface appears. Textures are image files that feed those properties with specific visual detail. For example, an Albedo texture gives the base color pattern, while a Normal map provides per-pixel surface perturbations that fake small bumps and grooves. Concretely, you can have a wooden bench model; the model defines the bench's shape, the material defines that the surface is wood-like, and an Albedo texture places the wood grain onto the material. A common misconception is to treat textures as standalone assets that directly change a mesh. Textures themselves do nothing without a material to interpret them. Another misconception is that Normal maps add geometry; they only alter lighting calculations to suggest geometry. Practice by creating a material named M_WoodFloor, assign a wood Albedo to the Albedo slot, then assign a Normal map and observe how perceived depth changes. Key takeaway: materials are the interpreters, textures supply the data.

keyIdea.title: Material vs Texture
keyIdea.text: Materials interpret how textures affect surface light response; textures are the image sources used by materials.

content.html:
Core Concept
Materials vs Textures
A material defines surface behavior under light. Textures are images that provide the material with color and micro detail.
Definition: Material — the surface's properties and how it responds to light.
Definition: Texture — an image file used as a map for Albedo, Normal, Metallic, Smoothness or AO.
Concrete example
A wooden bench uses a wood Albedo for color and a Normal map for grain; the material pairs these to render a believable wood surface.
Key takeaway
Textures need a material to be rendered; change textures by changing the material's map slots.
Illustrative cards
Material
Properties: Color, Metallic, Smoothness, Transparency
Controls light interaction and which textures are used.
Texture
Image maps: Albedo, Normal, Metallic, AO
Provide the specific visual data applied by the material.
Misconception
Normal maps create geometry. They do not; they alter surface normals to change lighting and imply detail without extra polygons.

screens.title: The Standard Shader and PBR
screens.narratorSegment: Unity's Standard shader is designed around Physically Based Rendering, or PBR, which models how light interacts with surfaces using physically inspired parameters. The goal of PBR is consistent appearance under different lighting conditions: a material authored once will look plausible whether viewed in bright sunlight or soft indoor lighting. Key PBR parameters include metallic and smoothness values that determine whether light reflects as colored metal highlights or white specular highlights from dielectrics. PBR enforces an energy-conserving relationship: a pixel cannot reflect more light than it receives. Practically, this means you should not boost both diffuse and specular to compensate; instead, author correct metallic maps and smoothness values. A concrete example: a steel pipe should have high metallicness and moderate smoothness so highlights reflect the pipe’s base color. A common misconception is that PBR makes everything look shiny; instead, PBR helps materials behave predictably. Mastery means using correct maps and sliders so the same asset fits multiple lighting setups without reauthoring. The Standard Shader and PBR means pbr supports realistic, consistent light response by using material parameters like metallic and smoothness under an energy-conserving model.. In practical terms, why unity's standard shader uses physically based rendering. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: PBR principle
keyIdea.text: PBR supports realistic, consistent light response by using material parameters like metallic and smoothness under an energy-conserving model.

content.html:
Definition
Standard Shader & PBR
The Standard shader exposes PBR parameters so materials respond to light realistically and consistently.
Metallic
Controls whether reflections carry the surface color (metals) or remain white (non-metals).
Smoothness
Controls how sharp or blurred reflections appear; higher smoothness gives mirror-like highlights.
Practical example
Author a metal with high metallic values and low roughness for polished steel, and for rusted parts lower metallic and smoothness to look rough and diffuse.
Why it matters
PBR lets you reuse materials across different scenes and lights. Proper maps make tuning minimal and predictable.
Misconception
PBR is not simply a shiny finish; it models energy flow so materials conserve light and behave predictably.
Check your work
Rotate the object under directional light and compare reflections with expected material type: metal should show colored reflections; wood should not.

screens.title: Albedo: Base Color and Brightness
screens.narratorSegment: The Albedo map defines the base color and diffuse brightness of a material. It’s the simplest texture map: a standard color image that represents the visible pattern and pigment of the surface. Importantly, Albedo should not contain baked lighting or shadow information if you intend it for PBR workflows, because PBR lighting is computed at runtime; baked shadows in the Albedo will look incorrect under different light setups. For a stone wall, the Albedo carries the color variation and mortar lines. A practical step: check that the Albedo texture does not have strong shading baked into it. A common mistake is using a shaded photograph as an Albedo; that creates double-shading once scene lighting is applied. When authoring Albedo, keep colors physically plausible and use AO maps to add subtle crevice darkening instead of burning that into the Albedo. To test, set the material’s Metallic to zero and Smoothness to a middle value, then toggle the Albedo on and off to see the map’s true contribution. Closing question: when you see unexpected dark spots, did the Albedo include baked shadows?

keyIdea.title: Albedo role
keyIdea.text: Albedo supplies base color without baked lighting; keep it clean so real-time lighting can do its work.

content.html:
Albedo Map
Base color and diffuse response
Albedo is the color image for the material. It should not contain baked shadows or lighting.
Concrete example
A brick Albedo provides red and mortar color. Ambient Occlusion map adds crevice shadowing rather than baking it into Albedo.
Misconception
Using a shaded photograph as Albedo is common but wrong for PBR; it bakes lighting into texture and conflicts with runtime lighting.
Quick test
Toggle Albedo on/off on a neutral material to verify the map supplies only color information.
Authoring tips
  • Keep Albedo free of strong shadows or highlights.
  • Use AO for crevice shadows instead of baked darkening on Albedo.
  • When in doubt, desaturate slightly to avoid color bleed in reflections.
Key takeaway
Albedo = pigment. Keep lighting out of it so PBR lighting remains accurate.

screens.title: Normal Maps: Fake Detail Without Geometry
screens.narratorSegment: Normal maps change the per-pixel surface normal used in lighting calculations so a flat mesh appears to have bumps and grooves. They are authored as special textures, usually with a dominant blue-purple tint, and must be marked as Normal Map in Unity’s import settings so the engine interprets them correctly. A practical example: a flat floor with a Normal map of wood grain will catch highlights and shadows that follow the grain, creating the illusion of depth without extra polygons. A common mistake is not setting the texture type to Normal Map; in that case Unity treats the image as a color map and the lighting will be wrong. Another issue is using a low-resolution normal map for a large surface: details will look blocky. To test a Normal map, enable and disable it on a neutral material and rotate a directional light; the perceived relief should shift convincingly. Finally, remember that Normal maps do not change silhouettes; large profile changes still require real geometry. Closing reflection: when you want micro detail with low cost, will a Normal map suffice or do you need displacement?

keyIdea.text: Normal maps alter lighting normals per-pixel to suggest surface detail without adding polygons; ensure Normal Map import type is set.

content.html:
Normal Map
Fake detail, real lighting change
Normals change the way a surface appears to catch light. They are essential for perceived depth without geometry.
Remember: Set texture Type to Normal Map in import settings so Unity processes it correctly.
Concrete example
Apply a wood-grain normal to a flat board to see highlights follow the grain, creating the illusion of depth.
Common mistake
Treating a normal image as a color texture or forgetting to mark it as Normal Map causes incorrect lighting and flat appearance.
Practical checks
  • Set Normal Map type and Apply in the Inspector.
  • Use adequate resolution for large surfaces to avoid blocky detail.
  • Remember Normal maps do not change silhouette; use real geometry for large offsets.
Key takeaway
Normal maps are a low-cost way to add convincing micro detail via lighting, not geometry.

screens.title: Metallic vs Dielectric; Smoothness explains reflections
screens.narratorSegment: Metallic and Smoothness are two complementary PBR parameters that shape reflections. The Metallic map marks which parts of a surface behave like metal and which behave like dielectrics. Metals reflect light and tint highlights with the object's base color; non-metals reflect white specular highlights and keep diffuse color in the Albedo. Smoothness controls how sharp or blurred those reflections are: high smoothness yields mirror-like highlights, low smoothness produces rough, soft reflections. Together they let you create complex surfaces — for example, a worn steel panel with rust: the metal areas should be metallic with higher smoothness where polished, while rusted spots are less metallic and rougher. A common misconception is swapping metallic and smoothness roles; they are distinct: metallic toggles metal behavior, smoothness controls microfacet roughness. To check your maps, look at reflection edges while rotating the object; metallic regions should carry color in the specular, non-metal regions should not. How will you represent surfaces with mixed metal and paint? The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Metallic toggles metal behavior; Smoothness adjusts reflection sharpness. Use both maps to represent mixed surfaces.

content.html:
Comparison
Metallic vs Dielectric
Metallic map marks metal behavior. Dielectrics keep diffuse color and white speculars.
Example: Rusted metal
Rust patches: lower metallic and lower smoothness. Exposed steel: higher metallic and higher smoothness for colored highlights.
Misconception
Smoothness is not the same as metallic. Increasing smoothness makes reflections sharper but does not change whether reflections carry base color.
Practical checks
  • Inspect metallic map values: 0 means dielectric, 1 means metal.
  • Use alpha channel of metallic map for smoothness when combined, or a separate smoothness map as needed.
  • Rotate object and watch colored highlights on metallic areas to verify correct behavior.
Key takeaway
Use metallic and smoothness together to model complex mixed surfaces realistically.

screens.title: Ambient Occlusion and Height Maps
screens.narratorSegment: Ambient Occlusion (AO) maps simulate areas where ambient light is occluded, such as crevices or tight corners, by darkening those regions. AO is a multiply map applied on top of Albedo or used in the occlusion slot to increase perceived depth without adding geometry. A Height map, sometimes used for parallax or displacement, encodes elevation and can produce stronger depth cues but may require extra shader support. AO is best for subtle, general depth; Height maps are for noticeable parallax effects. A practical example is a cobblestone surface: the AO map darkens mortar lines and the underside of stones, while a height map can be used sparingly for parallax on a close-up prop. A common mistake is baking strong, obvious AO into the Albedo rather than using an AO map; this reduces flexibility across lighting changes. When deciding which to use, prefer AO for soft shadowing in corners and height maps only when the shader or performance budget supports parallax or displacement. Ambient Occlusion and Height Maps means use ao for subtle crevice shading and height maps for stronger perceived depth when supported by the shader.. In practical terms, ao darkens crevices; height maps add parallax or displacement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use AO for subtle crevice shading and height maps for stronger perceived depth when supported by the shader.

content.html:
Ambient Occlusion
AO and Height Maps
AO darkens areas that receive less ambient light. Height maps can add parallax or displacement effects.
Concrete example
Use an AO map to darken mortar between stones. Use a height map only if the shader supports parallax or displacement for closer objects.
Common mistake
Baking AO into Albedo removes flexibility and causes incorrect shading under different lighting.
Practical tips
  • Place AO in the Occlusion slot to multiply with lighting for subtle depth.
  • Reserve height maps for props or close-up surfaces where parallax is noticeable.
  • Use compressed formats and appropriate Max Size to balance quality and memory.
Key takeaway
AO adds soft crevice shading; height maps add stronger depth but have higher cost or shader needs.

screens.title: Create a New Material and Assign Textures
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a PBR material in Unity is a short, repeatable process you should memorize. First, in the Project window right-click and choose Create → Material. Name it descriptively, for example M_RustedMetal_PBR, and place it in Assets/Materials for organization. With the new material selected, confirm the Shader dropdown is set to Standard. Next, drag the Albedo texture into the Albedo slot, the Metallic map into the Metallic Map slot, the Normal map into the Normal Map slot, and AO into the Occlusion slot. If Smoothness is provided in the alpha channel of the Metallic map, Unity will read it automatically; otherwise use a separate Smoothness map or the Smoothness slider. Configure your Normal map’s import type to Normal Map before assigning it. Finally, apply the material by dragging it onto a mesh in the Scene or into the Mesh Renderer materials array. A common oversight is skipping Normal map import settings or applying textures directly without a material. After applying, rotate lights and the object to verify depth and reflection behavior. Practice this flow until it is second nature. screens.title: Texture Import Settings and Inspector Checks
screens.narratorSegment: Before assigning a texture to a material, you must configure its import settings in the Project window. The most important settings are Texture Type for Normal maps, Max Size which caps resolution, Filter Mode to control sampling, and Wrap Mode for tiling. Mark a normal image as Normal Map so Unity processes it into a normal format. Max Size is used to reduce memory for distant or small props; lowering this value reduces G P U memory use but can increase visible pixelation. Filter Mode should often be Bilinear or Trilinear for smooth blending; Point filtering causes hard pixel edges useful for pixel-art but not most PBR textures. Wrap Mode set to Repeat is necessary when you want tiling textures on large surfaces. A common error is leaving a Normal map as Default and then wondering why lighting looks wrong. A practical check: open the texture in the Inspector, set Texture Type to Normal Map, set Filter Mode to Trilinear, enable Generate Mip Maps, set Wrap Mode to Repeat for tiling textures, and adjust Max Size to an appropriate power-of-two value. After applying, inspect the material again to see corrected shading. When you configure imports deliberately, you avoid many visual surprises.

fullNarratorScript:
In 3D rendering, the shape of a model is only half the story. The material is the surface definition that tells the renderer how that shape interacts with light. Textures are image maps that feed a material with color, bump, metalness and other surface detail. In this chapter you will learn how Unity’s Standard shader implements Physically Based Rendering, why separate maps like Albedo, Normal, Metallic and Smoothness matter, and how to avoid common mistakes like blurry or incorrectly imported textures. We will walk through creating a material, configuring texture import settings, and applying a PBR texture set to a model so you can see direct cause and effect. A practical focus will help you balance visual fidelity and performance when choosing texture resolution. By the end you’ll be able to create a PBR material, know what each map contributes, and fix frequent issues that make assets look wrong in a scene. Think of materials as the skin and textures as the decals that give that skin its specific, believable detail.

In this lesson you will gain four practical competencies that let you make and control believable surfaces in Unity. First, you will clearly differentiate materials from textures: the material defines how a surface responds to light while textures are image files that provide color and surface detail. Second, you will create and configure materials using the Standard shader, so you can author PBR-ready surfaces. Third, you will apply and interpret core texture maps — Albedo, Normal, Metallic, Smoothness, and Occlusion — and know how each affects the final rendering. Fourth, you will identify and correct common problems, such as blurry textures, wrong normal map import, or incorrect metallic values. Each objective connects to practical tasks: creating a material, setting a Normal Map import, dragging textures into slots, and inspecting the Mesh Renderer. These skills matter because they let you iterate quickly and keep scenes both realistic and performant. A quick mnemonic to remember the maps is: Color, Bump, Metal, Shine, Shade. Practice each step deliberately and verify the result under varied lighting.

This screen shows how to practice and verify each objective. For differentiation, open a simple model and compare two materials: one with only an Albedo texture and one with Albedo plus Normal and Metallic maps. Observe how depth and reflections change. For creating materials, practice by naming and organizing materials in a Materials folder, set the shader to Standard, and drag textures into their slots. For PBR maps, test by toggling the Metallic and Smoothness sliders to see how a surface moves from dielectric to metal-like behavior. For troubleshooting, intentionally reduce the texture Max Size and note pixelation, then correct it. Each practice session concludes with a quick verification: rotate the object under a directional light and check reflections, and inspect the Mesh Renderer to ensure the material is used and textured channels are populated. These checks will make your learning systematic and repeatable. A short checklist helps: Verify imports, verify slots, adjust sliders, and test under varied lighting.

A material is the set of properties that define how a surface looks and how it interacts with light. Think of it as the object's skin: it holds color values, reflective behavior, transparency, and how rough or smooth the surface appears. Textures are image files that feed those properties with specific visual detail. For example, an Albedo texture gives the base color pattern, while a Normal map provides per-pixel surface perturbations that fake small bumps and grooves. Concretely, you can have a wooden bench model; the model defines the bench's shape, the material defines that the surface is wood-like, and an Albedo texture places the wood grain onto the material. A common misconception is to treat textures as standalone assets that directly change a mesh. Textures themselves do nothing without a material to interpret them. Another misconception is that Normal maps add geometry; they only alter lighting calculations to suggest geometry. Practice by creating a material named M_WoodFloor, assign a wood Albedo to the Albedo slot, then assign a Normal map and observe how perceived depth changes. Key takeaway: materials are the interpreters, textures supply the data.

Unity's Standard shader is designed around Physically Based Rendering, or PBR, which models how light interacts with surfaces using physically inspired parameters. The goal of PBR is consistent appearance under different lighting conditions: a material authored once will look plausible whether viewed in bright sunlight or soft indoor lighting. Key PBR parameters include metallic and smoothness values that determine whether light reflects as colored metal highlights or white specular highlights from dielectrics. PBR enforces an energy-conserving relationship: a pixel cannot reflect more light than it receives. Practically, this means you should not boost both diffuse and specular to compensate; instead, author correct metallic maps and smoothness values. A concrete example: a steel pipe should have high metallicness and moderate smoothness so highlights reflect the pipe’s base color. A common misconception is that PBR makes everything look shiny; instead, PBR helps materials behave predictably. Mastery means using correct maps and sliders so the same asset fits multiple lighting setups without reauthoring. The Standard Shader and PBR means pbr supports realistic, consistent light response by using material parameters like metallic and smoothness under an energy-conserving model.. In practical terms, why unity's standard shader uses physically based rendering. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Albedo map defines the base color and diffuse brightness of a material. It’s the simplest texture map: a standard color image that represents the visible pattern and pigment of the surface. Importantly, Albedo should not contain baked lighting or shadow information if you intend it for PBR workflows, because PBR lighting is computed at runtime; baked shadows in the Albedo will look incorrect under different light setups. For a stone wall, the Albedo carries the color variation and mortar lines. A practical step: check that the Albedo texture does not have strong shading baked into it. A common mistake is using a shaded photograph as an Albedo; that creates double-shading once scene lighting is applied. When authoring Albedo, keep colors physically plausible and use AO maps to add subtle crevice darkening instead of burning that into the Albedo. To test, set the material’s Metallic to zero and Smoothness to a middle value, then toggle the Albedo on and off to see the map’s true contribution. Closing question: when you see unexpected dark spots, did the Albedo include baked shadows?

Normal maps change the per-pixel surface normal used in lighting calculations so a flat mesh appears to have bumps and grooves. They are authored as special textures, usually with a dominant blue-purple tint, and must be marked as Normal Map in Unity’s import settings so the engine interprets them correctly. A practical example: a flat floor with a Normal map of wood grain will catch highlights and shadows that follow the grain, creating the illusion of depth without extra polygons. A common mistake is not setting the texture type to Normal Map; in that case Unity treats the image as a color map and the lighting will be wrong. Another issue is using a low-resolution normal map for a large surface: details will look blocky. To test a Normal map, enable and disable it on a neutral material and rotate a directional light; the perceived relief should shift convincingly. Finally, remember that Normal maps do not change silhouettes; large profile changes still require real geometry. Closing reflection: when you want micro detail with low cost, will a Normal map suffice or do you need displacement?

Metallic and Smoothness are two complementary PBR parameters that shape reflections. The Metallic map marks which parts of a surface behave like metal and which behave like dielectrics. Metals reflect light and tint highlights with the object's base color; non-metals reflect white specular highlights and keep diffuse color in the Albedo. Smoothness controls how sharp or blurred those reflections are: high smoothness yields mirror-like highlights, low smoothness produces rough, soft reflections. Together they let you create complex surfaces — for example, a worn steel panel with rust: the metal areas should be metallic with higher smoothness where polished, while rusted spots are less metallic and rougher. A common misconception is swapping metallic and smoothness roles; they are distinct: metallic toggles metal behavior, smoothness controls microfacet roughness. To check your maps, look at reflection edges while rotating the object; metallic regions should carry color in the specular, non-metal regions should not. How will you represent surfaces with mixed metal and paint? Metallic vs Dielectric; Smoothness explains reflections means metallic toggles metal behavior; smoothness adjusts reflection sharpness. use both maps to represent mixed surfaces.. Ambient Occlusion (AO) maps simulate areas where ambient light is occluded, such as crevices or tight corners, by darkening those regions. AO is a multiply map applied on top of Albedo or used in the occlusion slot to increase perceived depth without adding geometry. A Height map, sometimes used for parallax or displacement, encodes elevation and can produce stronger depth cues but may require extra shader support. AO is best for subtle, general depth; Height maps are for noticeable parallax effects. A practical example is a cobblestone surface: the AO map darkens mortar lines and the underside of stones, while a height map can be used sparingly for parallax on a close-up prop. A common mistake is baking strong, obvious AO into the Albedo rather than using an AO map; this reduces flexibility across lighting changes. When deciding which to use, prefer AO for soft shadowing in corners and height maps only when the shader or performance budget supports parallax or displacement. Many visual problems stem from a few repeatable mistakes that are quick to check and fix. If a texture appears blurry or pixelated, first inspect the texture’s Max Size in import settings and ensure Mip Maps are enabled. Low Max Size or missing mip maps cause softness, especially at distance. If normal lighting looks wrong, open the texture and confirm its Texture Type is set to Normal Map so Unity converts it correctly. When reflections look strange or color appears in highlights where it shouldn’t, verify the Metallic map: metals should have white areas in the metallic map and dielectrics black. Another common case is using the wrong Filter Mode; Point filtering can create visible pixel edges. To summarize, remember three core ideas. First, materials are the surface definitions that decide how geometry responds to light; textures are image maps that populate those materials with color, normals, metalness, smoothness and ambient occlusion. Second, Unity’s Standard shader implements PBR: metallic and smoothness control whether reflections carry color and how sharp they are, while normal maps fake micro-detail and AO adds soft crevice shading. Third, a consistent workflow — correct texture import settings, proper Normal map type, appropriate Max Size, and verified Mesh Renderer assignment — prevents most common problems like blurriness or incorrect shading.
